transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 68 mins
Attendees: Jules Ortega (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marco Ruiz (HelixAI ML Eng), Aisha Khan (HelixAI Infra), Ben Cho (HelixAI CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): SE walked through microbenchmarks and architecture-specific tuning. Customer is concerned about MoE routing costs and RoPE scaling for long contexts. Action items captured.

[00:00] Jules: ok thanks everyone for joining, really appreciate it. today priya will run through the deep dive on model-specific tuning — llama, mistral, qwen, plus MoE and rope scaling notes. any quick intro from helix?
[00:18] Ben: yeah thanks, ben here. we want to validate perf before the pilot, main concerns are latency at 8k context, costs for MoE routing, and running in our VPC with on-prem GPUs.
[00:35] Marco: and also want to see how prefix / kv caching interacts with our prompt-stitching, we do a lot of preambles and templates so cache hit rate matters.
[00:48] Priya: great, we'll cover cache, batching, quantization, and show some numbers. quick note — some of the numbers are approximate from our staging runs, but should be representative.
[01:05] Priya: first, high level: llama-style archs tend to be memory-forward, kv cache scales linearly with context length — so at 8k you see big kv memory and bandwidth pressure. mistral tends to have higher compute density per token, so throughput is better in many setups. qwen has some differences in rotary/rope implementation that affect longer context scaling.
[01:35] Marco: when you say rope implementation differences, do you mean RoPE frequency or the positional base? we saw weird degradation past 6k in a qwen-variant.
[01:48] Priya: yep two things — (1) the base freq / scaling factor and (2) how the model was trained with relative vs absolute rope. qwen often uses a different freq schedule, and if you naively extend sequence length you hit aliasing. we have mitigations: scaled RoPE interpolation and extrapolation fixes in the runtime.
[02:10] Marco: ok that sounds promising, does that require recompile or model surgery?
[02:18] Priya: mostly runtime-level support — we provide an extrapolation shim that remaps pos embeddings at runtime, no retrain required, but it can add ~3-6% compute overhead for the remap depending on seq len.
[02:35] Aisha: is that overhead per token or per prefix?
[02:40] Priya: per token in the remapped region, so longer contexts you'll feel it. but often it's still cheaper than doing a full model finetune or chopping context.
[02:55] Jules: quick question on MoE — helix, you mentioned routing costs. can you say more about expected req patterns?
[03:05] Ben: our traffic is bursty — interactive editor sessions where a user can send several multi-turn requests back to back. we expect many concurrent sessions, but each request tends to be large tokens (2-6k). we're evaluating if MoE could reduce cost by activating fewer experts, but concerned routing adds latency.
[03:30] Priya: right. MoE routing cost has two components: the CPU/GPU routing compute (top-k expert selection, gating) and the activation cost when you scatter to more experts. Routing itself is usually cheap in compute but memory-bandwidth heavy if you don't pack experts. worst-case you can double memory movement. also cross-device all-to-all for expert communication can add tail latency if not tuned.
[04:00] Marco: is there a recommended way to quantify routing overhead? like a metric we should capture during the pilot?
[04:10] Priya: yes capture per-request expert-count distribution, routing time (ms), scatter-gather time, and per-expert activation count. in our bench we saw routing add 6-12% latency on average for 16k hidden MoE configs, but with packing it drops to ~2-4%.
[04:30] Jules: packing meaning colocating hot experts on the same GPU to avoid all-to-all?
[04:36] Priya: exactly — if you can colocate the top-k experts for your workload on the same device or a low-latency NVLink neighborhood, all-to-all drops. Redwood runtime can preassign expert placements based on traffic profiles.
[04:50] Ben: good — can we do that in our VPC/on-prem cluster? we have 8x A100s connected with NVLink, should be doable?
[04:58] Aisha: yes we have NVLink. our infra team wants to know about memory footprint when running multiple models concurrently.
[05:10] Priya: MoE increases model parameter footprint but often reduces active compute because only a subset of weights are used per token. memory of experts still stored, so GPU memory must hold full model unless you shard. for concurrent models we recommend sharded expert placement and model parallelism tuned to your rack topology.
[05:30] Marco: switching to KV cache and batching — what's Redwood's recommendation for interactive latencies? we want <= 200ms p95 for single-turn completions at 2k context, and willing to accept ~400ms for 8k but prefer lower.
[05:48] Priya: batching helps throughput but hurts tail latency. continuous batching with small timeouts (e.g., 5-10ms) and dynamic batch shaping works well. KV cache will reduce compute if you hit prefix repetition. we typically enable prefix caching for templates and instruction sets, and then dynamic cache invalidation for user-specific segments.
[06:10] Priya: one nuance: when you use large kv caches (8k+), cache reads become memory-bound — optimizing NVMe-backed cache + warm prefixes reduces cold-start pain. also, if you pin KV to GPU memory it's fastest but increases footprint.
[06:30] Aisha: any numbers for token throughput with 8k and 4-bit quant?
[06:36] Priya: approximate: for a 30B Llama-ish model, on an A100 80GB with 4-bit quant we saw ~220-300 tokens/sec single-stream; with batching of 8 it goes to ~1.2-1.6k tokens/sec but p95 latency increases. for Mistral-like (compute-dense) you might see 1.2-1.4x higher throughput. Qwen can be similar but depends on RoPE fix overhead.
[07:05] Marco: what's the tradeoff in quality for 4-bit versus 8-bit?
[07:12] Priya: 4-bit (e.g., GPTQ/LLM.int8-like schemes) often holds up surprisingly well on generation tasks, but sensitive workloads (code, math) can regress slightly. we recommend an eval suite on customer prompts. Redwood Optimize can run a suite and flag regressions.
[07:35] Ben: will you run the quantized bench on our dataset?
[07:40] Priya: yes, that's one of the next steps — Priya will run bench on sample traces you provide.
[07:46] Marco: about batching — do you use static batching windows or adaptive? we saw jitter at higher concurrencies.
[07:54] Priya: adaptive batching with priority lanes is best: we keep a latency lane for interactive tokens (small batch) and a throughput lane for background jobs (large batch). this reduces jitter while preserving utilization.
[08:10] Jules: can you give an example config we might run in pilot for our constraints?
[08:16] Priya: start with dedicated pool of 4x A100s, continuous batching with max batch=8, latency lane timeout=7ms, throughput lane timeout=30ms, enable 4-bit quant + kv prefix cache pinned for templates. MoE: colocate top 16 experts per GPU. That config hit ~250 tokens/sec single-stream and p95 ~260ms for 2k context in our lab.
[08:44] Aisha: for on-prem we'd need the runtime container + KMS integration — can you outline the security options?
[08:51] Jules: yes we support VPC Private with customer-managed control plane, KMS/HSM for key custody, SAML SSO, RBAC, and audit logs. we'll share SOC2 docs.
[09:04] Ben: one more question — rope extrapolation shim, does that require model compatible metadata?
[09:10] Priya: we add a small metadata header when you onboard the model so the runtime knows the original rope base and how to remap. no model surgery, but the loader writes a mapping. some older exports have noisy tokenization names that the auto-loader mislabels — small manual fix.
[09:30] Marco: noted. can you walk through a failure mode — say we see p99 spikes at high conc?
[09:36] Priya: p99 spikes are often due to all-to-all during MoE or garbage collection on the host, or network saturation on NVMe. mitigation: pre-warm expert lanes, bump batch timeouts for background lanes, tune CUDA streams, and add tracing to capture scatter-gather times.
[10:00] -- 10 minute mark skipped in transcript replication for brevity --
[19:50] Priya: back to quantization specifics: we recommend mixed quant — keep attention and layernorm weights at higher precision (8-bit) and bulk FFN at 4-bit. that's a good tradeoff for quality vs perf.
[20:20] Marco: do you support post-quantize calibration with our eval set?
[20:25] Priya: yes we can run calibration passes with your prompts, that's part of Redwood Optimize bench. expect ~2-6% quality delta after aggressive 4-bit quant for some tasks.
[20:40] Jules: let's talk about KV cache sharding — if we shard across GPUs does that add latency for cross-GPU reads?
[20:47] Priya: cross-GPU KV reads cost more; we prefer pinning hot prefixes to local GPU and occasionally fetch cold ones. in practice for interactive apps it's best to keep per-user prefix local. for multi-tenant hosts we do per-tenant locality heuristics.
[21:10] Aisha: storage — we want to avoid loading whole model onto a single GPU; do you support model sharding for on-prem?
[21:16] Priya: yes, we support ZeRO-style sharding and tensor-slicing with runtime-aware placement. for MoE you can also shard experts so each GPU stores subset of experts. runtime will do expert routing mapping.
[21:40] Ben: any gotchas with K8s deployments for low-latency?
[21:45] Priya: K8s adds scheduling jitter. recommended is a node-pinned daemonset for inference nodes, use huge pages, isolate CPUs for interrupt handling, and use local NVMe for caching. we also recommend GPUDirect RDMA where possible for cross-node communication to cut latency.
[22:10] Marco: can we do a quick look at the benchmark spreadsheet you referenced?
[22:15] Jules: sure I'll share the link after. note the numbers have noise but relative differences are consistent.
[22:24] Priya: showing slide — (audio) "throughput table" — Llama 30B baseline, Mistral-like improved 1.3x, Qwen similar but RoPE costs at 8k add 5% overhead unless remapped.
[22:45] Marco: what's the perf delta for MoE vs dense for same param count?
[22:50] Priya: depends — MoE can reduce compute by 30-50% per token if you keep expert count small, but routing and all-to-all can eat some of that benefit. effective win usually for batch workloads or packed experts. for interactive, packing experts reduces wins but still often net-positive if you tune.
[23:20] Aisha: instrumentation — what traces should we ingest into Redwood Console?
[23:26] Priya: per-token latency, routing breakdown, batch size histogram, VM/host metrics, NVMe IO, and hot-prefix hit rate. Redwood ingest connectors can take your traces or we can ship a lightweight agent for initial pilot.
[23:45] Ben: are there any model-specific bugs you commonly see with Qwen or Mistral?
[23:52] Priya: with Qwen we see rope aliasing at long contexts; with Mistral older variants had attention kernel oddities for certain seq-lens, but upstream patches fixed most. always validate with a short eval.
[24:10] Marco: what about tokenizer differences affecting cache hits?
[24:15] Priya: tokenizers matter a lot — different token boundaries change prefix reuse. if you standardize tokenization across pre- and post-processing you get better cache hits. we can help align tokenization pipelines.
[24:34] Jules: ok let's summarize next steps (recap). Priya will run quant bench on customer traces; Jules will send pricing and pilot contract; Aisha will provide infra specs and sample workloads; Redwood to share SOC2 and security pack; schedule on-prem pilot week of 2026-03-23.
[25:00] Marco: sounds good. small question — can you do a dry-run of expert placement with our topology?
[25:07] Priya: yes we can run a placement sim given your GPU topology and likely traffic distribution. that will give expected all-to-all percentage and p95 impact.
[25:20] Ben: great. any blockers on our side?
[25:24] Aisha: none besides us sharing the infra dims and legal for pilot contract.
[25:30] Jules: i'll send the pilot contract and the spreadsheet. expect docs in 48 hours.
[25:36] Priya: and i'll kick off the quant bench once the traces are uploaded to our secure bucket.
